hypothesis: Adding an ADX trend strength filter and a minimum ATR volatility filter should suppress entries during strong trends or low‑volatility periods, which were causing frequent whipsaws and large drawdowns in the pure Bollinger mean‑reversion approach, thereby improving win rate and Sharpe ratio while preserving the core mean‑reversion edge.

Adding an ATR‑based distance filter ensures we only enter when the price is materially beyond the Bollinger lower/upper band, which filters out shallow touches that often reverse quickly; coupling this with an ADX > 20 trend filter confines trades to low‑trend, ranging environments where mean‑reversion is more reliable, thereby reducing prolonged adverse moves and the observed high drawdown.

When price drops sharply below the lower Bollinger band it is likely over‑extended and will revert toward the mean; using the middle band as an exit captures the reversion, while ATR‑based stop‑loss and take‑profit scale risk to the current volatility, reducing premature exits in low‑volatility periods.

Adding an ADX weak‑trend filter to the Bollinger‑band mean‑reversion signal prevents entries during strong trends, which were the main cause of the large drawdowns; combined with ATR‑based stop‑loss/take‑profit this should reduce loss magnitude while preserving the mean‑reversion edge.

Adding a volatility filter (ATR > minimum) ensures trades are only taken in sufficiently active markets, while requiring a true price cross below the lower Bollinger band reduces premature entries; exiting when price reaches the middle band captures the mean-reversion target, together improving win rate and limiting drawdown.

Adding an ADX filter (adx < 25) restricts entries to low‑trend regimes, preventing the mean‑reversion trades from being caught in strong trends that cause large losses; this should cut the excessive drawdown while preserving the Bollinger‑band reversal edge.
